lines: Build a real buffer pool: a frame table, a pin count on each frame, and a dirty bit on each frame.
Now pin every single frame in that pool, and try to load one more page than the pool can actually hold.
What happens?
answer: There is nothing left in it that can be evicted; a pinned frame is simply never a candidate.

lines: Run it for real: with every frame genuinely pinned, loading one more page than the pool can hold was rejected outright.
Nothing was evicted, because nothing could be.
Now unpin those frames, and load a new page. One of them gets evicted to make room.
If the frame that gets evicted happens to be dirty, does its own data get written back first, before that frame is handed to the new page?
answer: Nothing dirty is ever simply discarded along with the frame.

lines: Run it for real: the dirty frame's own data was genuinely written back first, and only afterward was that same frame reused for the new page.
steps.takeaway: A dirty frame's own data is never simply discarded; it's written back first, before its frame is reused.

lines: Now give the real eviction policy, CLOCK, an actual choice.
Take two unpinned frames: touch one of them again since the last sweep, and leave the other one genuinely alone.
Load one more page.
Does CLOCK evict the one just touched again, or the one left untouched?
answer: Being touched again buys a real second chance.

lines: Run it for real: CLOCK genuinely evicted the frame left untouched since the last sweep, and spared the one that had been accessed again.
steps.takeaway: CLOCK's own reference bit gives a touched frame a real second chance; an untouched one doesn't get one.

lines: One real system names exactly these fields on its own real shared buffer: whether it's dirty, its own clock-sweep count, and how many backends are pinning it right now.
What's that pinning count actually there to protect?
answer: Exactly the pin count this topic's own pool uses.
A frame being pinned right now is the entire reason it survives eviction.

lines: In that system's own words: the pinning count is how many backends currently hold that buffer pinned, and its own eviction function only ever touches a buffer nobody is pinning.
An earlier chapter's own approach to this same problem hands the question of when a dirty page actually gets written back to the operating system entirely.

A real paper on exactly that approach names the difference directly: the operating system can flush a dirty page back to disk at any moment it chooses, whether or not the write that dirtied it has even finished.
steps.takeaway: An explicit buffer pool decides for itself when a dirty page is written back; mmap hands that to the OS.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: a pinned frame is never a candidate for eviction, a dirty frame is always written back before its own frame gets reused, and a real sweep-based policy genuinely favors whichever frame was touched more recently.
A real system names exactly these same three things on its own shared buffers.
And where one approach hands the timing of a dirty write entirely to the operating system, an explicit pool like this one decides that for itself, on its own terms.
